newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn tax reform changes alienate big business.
newsitem.headline: Bonn tax reform changes alienate big business.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's battered coalition, by making late changes to its tax reforms to raise extra cash from big business, has alienated one of the few allies it has left on Germany's lobby-ridden political scene.

Newspapers on Monday were filled with attacks from business leaders on amendments pushed through by coalition parties in parliament's finance committee which would hit power utilities hardest, and also sharply limit tax writeoffs on company losses.
Hans-Olaf Henkel, chairman of the BDI industry federation, called the changes a "scandal", while BASF chairman Juergen Strube said the Kohl coalition had "lost control".

Industry leaders had lobbied in favour of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's original plan to cut top-rate corporation tax from 45 percent now to 35 percent by 1999, while simplifying the tax system by scrapping a plethora of exemptions.

Their reasoning was that, even though the reforms would not bring significant net tax cuts for business, cutting Germany's high company tax rate would encourage investment and help reduce unemployment which is now more than 11 percent.
But, with the changes announced last week, that arithmetic goes out of the window.

"If Bonn decides to go ahead with plans that increase rather than reduce the tax burden on industry there is going to be trouble," newsweekly Der Spiegel quoted Hans Peter Stihl, head of the Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT) as saying.

Power generators have threatened legal action after hearing that the loss of exemptions on reserves built up to pay to shut down nuclear plants would cost them four billion marks ($2.3 billion) in 1998.

The second change to the tax reform would halve the limit on tax writeoffs allowed against loss-carryovers -- a change costing big firms 1.6 billion marks but leaving the so-called "Mittelstand" of small- and medium-sized companies alone.

Defending the government's position against the barrage of criticism, finance committee chairman Carl-Ludwig Thiele wrote in a letter on Monday to business leaders that the Mittelstand would not be hit by the amendments.

But newspapers said the centre-right government had scored an own-goal by trying to extract extra cash from its natural allies in business to help Bonn reach borrowing targets for Europe's single currency.
"The coalition is doing its best finally to gamble away its last mark: the business view that it is more financially competent than the opposition," the Handelsblatt daily wrote.

Kohl will have realised that Germany is lagging countries like the U.S. and Britain in the reform race. Worse, the window of opportunity for reforms is closing because of the government's budget crisis, the newspaper added.
"One day a new 'grand tax reform' will return to the agenda -- but then the way will lead through a closed window. That will hurt," Handelsblatt said.

The latest changes also have done nothing to create an all-party consensus which would enable the tax reform to pass through the upper house of parliament, where the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) can veto tax legislation.

So, although Waigel's tax bills will pass their second and third readings in the Bundestag lower house this Thursday, certain rejection in the second chamber will lead to lengthy horse-trading in parliament's conflict resolution process. ($ = 1.729 German Marks)
